rules.when: a tiny or surgical change in a known place: a rename, an obvious one-file or config edit, mechanical cleanup, or a quick factual question about how something already works. If it needs a design decision, touches more than one coherent unit, or requires new tests or non-trivial logic, that is IMPLEMENT instead, not QUICK.
rules.why: Claude practical capacity is about 20 versus GPT's about 5 on this fleet - roughly 4:1, not 20:1 - so the smallest ordinary lane defaults to Claude Haiku rather than spending scarcer GPT headroom on trivial work. Haiku and Luna are genuinely interchangeable same-tier candidates for this bucket (both cheap, both low effort, neither semantically preferred over the other) so FirstMate's quota-array procedure may resolve between them after this rule matches. Escalate to anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 at low or medium, by explicit captain choice, only if the task needs more reasoning than either cheap-tier model comfortably gives - never Astra or Opus for ordinary quick work; those are reserved for genuinely hard reasoning (DEEP) or broad sustained execution (IMPLEMENT-LARGE). QUICK versus IMPLEMENT is a size/decision test, not a keyword match: a rename is QUICK, a rename that also requires touching call sites across a module and deciding a new interface is IMPLEMENT.

rules.when: read-only reconnaissance inside our own repository: finding files, callers, existing patterns, an inventory of something, or where a capability is implemented, with no external research and no code changes. If the question is about an external library, API, framework, or standard rather than our own code, that is RESEARCH instead.
rules.why: Ordinary in-repo recon is cheap, bounded work: Haiku at low effort reads and reports without needing deep synthesis. Luna at low effort is a genuinely interchangeable same-tier peer here too, the same capacity-aware pairing QUICK already uses, so FirstMate's quota-array procedure may resolve between them - never Sol, Astra, or Opus for ordinary exploration; those buy nothing a careful read does not already give here. EXPLORE never leaves this repository's own source; RESEARCH is aimed at documentation, APIs, or code outside it - that is the line between them.

rules.when: the same read-only, in-repository reconnaissance as ordinary EXPLORE above, but the reasoning is materially harder than a lookup - for example an unusually tangled call graph, or untangling behavior across many indirection layers. This is a separate, more specific rule within EXPLORE, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick this rule only when the harder-reasoning condition genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: Sonnet at medium effort is the deliberate escalation once plain reading stops being enough, still well short of RESEARCH's external-synthesis effort or DEEP's reasoning-difficulty bar - this is still in-repository recon, just harder recon.

rules.when: questions that require looking outside our own repository: external documentation, third-party APIs, dependency behavior, framework or protocol semantics, standards, or comparing our approach against upstream/OSS source. If the target is our own code rather than an external system, that is EXPLORE instead; if the deliverable is a judgment on a proposed change rather than an information-gathering pass, that is REVIEW instead.
rules.why: Sonnet at medium effort is the honest default for synthesizing external material.

rules.when: the same external-research work as ordinary RESEARCH above, specifically when Pi's own tooling (its research-oriented extensions or browsing) is materially better suited to the research target than a cold OMP session. This is a tooling condition, a separate more specific rule, never a default fallback chosen by quota.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-sol directly replaces the retired gpt-5.6-sol here. Sol on Pi is the deliberate route once Pi's own tooling is the better fit for the research target: it fits Pi's tooling profile for this specific job better than a cold OMP session would, at the same medium effort as the OMP default.

rules.when: ordinary review of code, a diff, a proposal, or a completion claim for correctness, maintainability, or regression risk - not adversarial challenge, not a structural/architecture decision, and not a deep root-cause investigation. If the deliverable is external information-gathering rather than judgment on our own change, that is RESEARCH instead; if independence from the author is the point, that is TENTH-MAN instead; if the question is about system boundaries or long-term structure, that is ARCHITECTURE instead. If the diff itself is complex enough to risk subtle regressions, concurrency bugs, or spans a broad cross-layer diff, that is the complex-REVIEW rule below instead; if the change is release-critical or touches auth/security, payments, migrations, or otherwise carries a high blast radius, that is the high-risk-REVIEW rule below instead.
rules.why: Medium effort covers an ordinary review. REVIEW stays on the same OMP session/harness family as implementation because it is not seeking independence - that is what separates it from TENTH-MAN, which deliberately runs on Pi, away from the implementation session. REVIEW also never owns a structural verdict about boundaries or migrations; that judgment belongs to ARCHITECTURE. Genuinely harder or riskier review scope is a separate, more specific rule below (complex or high-risk REVIEW), never a quota-resolved peer of this ordinary case.

rules.when: the same ordinary REVIEW work above, specifically when the diff itself is complex enough to risk subtle regressions, concurrency or race-condition bugs, or spans a broad cross-layer diff touching many coordinated pieces at once. This is a separate, more specific rule within REVIEW, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick it only when the complexity condition genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: High effort is the deliberate escalation once the diff's own complexity - subtle regressions, concurrency, or broad cross-layer scope - genuinely exceeds what medium effort comfortably covers, the same Sonnet-high lane IMPLEMENT-LARGE already validates.

rules.when: the same REVIEW work above, specifically for release-critical changes or work touching authentication/security, payments, migrations, or otherwise carrying a high blast radius if the review misses something. This is a separate, more specific rule within REVIEW, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary or complex case: pick it only when the stakes genuinely warrant it, not by default.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at high effort is reserved for review where the cost of a missed defect is highest - release-critical, auth/security, payment, migration, or otherwise high-blast-radius changes. Specialist skills such as Thermos remain independently selectable on top of this lane through the normal skill-selection path (primary-policy.md section 2); picking one never starts a second orchestration framework or supervisor identity. A cross-family second reviewer is a separate, more specific rule below, reached for only when an independent-family second opinion is genuinely warranted in addition to this primary review, never a default.

rules.when: the same release-critical or high-blast-radius REVIEW work above, specifically when an independent, cross-family second reviewer is warranted in addition to the Opus 5.5 primary review - the highest-stakes cases where a single reviewer's model family should not be the only check. This is a separate, more specific rule within REVIEW, not a quota-resolved peer of the primary high-risk case: pick it only when that additional independent-family need genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-sol on Pi is REVIEW's cross-family second reviewer, reached for only when the highest-stakes case above genuinely needs an independent, differently-sourced check in addition to the Opus 5.5 primary review, never as a routine substitute for it.

rules.when: structural decisions with real blast radius: a system or module boundary, an API or domain boundary, a data model, a migration shape, or any ambiguous design with long-term consequences. Use role architecture. If the deliverable is approval or risk-flagging of someone else's proposal rather than an independent structural recommendation, that is REVIEW instead; if the trigger is a hard-to-diagnose bug or subtle reasoning problem rather than a forward design decision, that is DEEP instead. If the decision is exceptional enough to warrant the strongest available reasoning and an independent second opinion, that is the exceptional-architecture rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Opus 5.5 at high effort is the default for structural decisions with real blast radius. Consultation here never automatically owns the implementation that follows. Escalate to the exceptional-architecture rule below, not this one, once the decision itself is exceptional rather than merely structural.

rules.when: the same structural-decision ARCHITECTURE work above, specifically when the decision is exceptional: unusually high stakes, unusually deep ambiguity, or a genuine need for an independent second opinion beyond the ordinary structural case. This is a separate, more specific rule within ARCHITECTURE, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick it only when the exceptional condition genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5 on OMP at xhigh and openai-codex/gpt-6-sol on Pi at xhigh are active xhigh peers for exceptional architecture; FirstMate resolves between them through the quota-array procedure after this rule matches. Sol especially serves as an independent second opinion, on a different harness and model family from the primary OMP session, at the lowest cost that still satisfies that independence. openai-codex/gpt-6-astra remains reserved for the separate, more specific ultra-exceptional rule below, reached for only when even this Sol pairing is not enough - never a routine peer here.

rules.when: the same exceptional ARCHITECTURE work above, specifically on the rare occasion even the Opus 5.5/Sol exceptional pairing above is not enough: the decision is so consequential or so deeply contested that the strongest available independent reasoning is warranted regardless of cost. This is a separate, more specific rule within ARCHITECTURE, not a quota-resolved peer of either case above: pick it only when that ultra-exceptional condition genuinely applies, never by default and never merely because the exceptional rule already matched.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-astra on Pi at xhigh is reached for only on this narrowest, most consequential tier of architecture decision, once the Opus 5.5/Sol exceptional pairing above is not enough. Astra stays limited to this and this configuration's other genuinely exceptional lanes; it is never a routine architecture default.

rules.when: deliberate adversarial challenge: an independent second opinion, a stress test of a plan's assumptions and failure modes, or scrutiny of a completion claim before an expensive or hard-to-reverse commitment - specifically when the work under review was primarily produced by a Claude/Anthropic model. Use role tenth-man. Never routine; risk-triggered or explicitly requested. If the goal is ordinary correctness/maintainability feedback rather than adversarial challenge, that is REVIEW instead; if the goal is a forward structural recommendation rather than challenging an existing one, that is ARCHITECTURE instead.
rules.why: Model-family diversity is the whole point: when the primary author is a Claude/Anthropic model, the challenger runs on Pi with GPT-6 Sol, a different provider and a different harness from the OMP session that likely produced the work, at the lowest cost that still satisfies family diversity. GPT-6 Astra remains available as a separate, more specific escalation below for the most critical or unresolved cases, never a routine default. TENTH-MAN versus DEEP: DEEP investigates why something is broken; TENTH-MAN challenges whether a plan or a completion claim actually holds, broken or not.

rules.when: the same deliberate adversarial-challenge TENTH-MAN work above, specifically when the primary author is still a Claude/Anthropic model and the Sol challenge above leaves the matter critical or genuinely unresolved - not merely difficult, but a case where the stakes or the ambiguity demand the strongest available cross-family challenger. This is a separate, more specific rule within TENTH-MAN, not a routine default: pick it only after the Sol challenge above has genuinely left the matter unresolved, never as a first choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-astra on Pi is reached for only as the most critical or unresolved escalation once the Sol challenge above is not enough, preserving TENTH-MAN's Claude-primary family-diversity route while keeping Astra an explicit, rarely-selected escalation rather than a routine default.

rules.when: the same deliberate adversarial-challenge TENTH-MAN work above, specifically when the work under review was primarily produced by an Astra or other OpenAI-codex model. This is a separate, more specific rule within TENTH-MAN, chosen by which model produced the work under review, not by quota: never let the same provider both author and adversarially review a piece of work.
rules.why: When the primary author is Astra or another OpenAI-codex model, the challenger switches to OMP with Opus 5.5 at xhigh so the reviewer's model family never matches the author's. This enforces the same independence TENTH-MAN's Claude-primary rule enforces, just from the other direction.

rules.when: ordinary bounded engineering: a feature, a bug fix, normal debugging, a normal refactor, or writing/repairing tests, with a blast radius you can hold in your head. This is the main coding lane and the unmarked default for real code changes. If the change is a one-file mechanical edit or a factual question, that is QUICK instead; if it spans many files or the design is not settled yet, that is IMPLEMENT-LARGE instead; if the change is primarily frontend/browser-visible behavior, that is UI/BROWSER instead. If the implementation itself is delicate - races, state machines, security-sensitive logic, or coordinated multi-file changes that must stay consistent - that is the complex-IMPLEMENT rule below instead.
rules.why: The everyday coding lane: OMP + Sonnet at medium effort. This is the default assumption for 'write code' work; only move to a neighboring category when one of its specific triggers actually applies, not because the request feels bigger or smaller than usual. Genuinely delicate implementation is a separate, more specific rule below (complex IMPLEMENT), never a quota-resolved peer of this ordinary case.

rules.when: the same ordinary bounded-engineering IMPLEMENT work above, specifically when the implementation itself is delicate: races and concurrency, state machines, security-sensitive logic, or coordinated multi-file changes that must stay consistent with each other. This is a separate, more specific rule within IMPLEMENT, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick it only when the delicacy condition genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: High effort is the deliberate escalation once the implementation itself - not just its size - is delicate enough that medium effort risks a subtle mistake: races, state machines, security-sensitive logic, or coordinated multi-file consistency.

rules.when: broad multi-file or long-horizon implementation where the direction is mostly already known - more files than IMPLEMENT, but not an unsettled reasoning problem. If the change is small enough to hold in your head, that is IMPLEMENT instead; if the difficulty is in figuring out what is wrong or what is true rather than in the amount of settled work to do, that is DEEP instead.
rules.why: Sonnet at high effort is the default for broad, mostly-settled execution.

rules.when: the same broad, mostly-settled IMPLEMENT-LARGE work above, specifically when the sheer sustained execution - not merely the file count - justifies a stronger model: a long autonomous run across many coordinated changes where Sonnet-high's throughput is genuinely the limiting factor. This is a separate, more specific rule, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case; do not pick it, and never pick Astra, just because many files are touched.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 here is difficult execution, not difficult reasoning - that is what separates this escalation from DEEP's Opus/Sol/Astra lanes. Opus 5.5 directly replaces Opus 5 in this lane. Escalate to xhigh, by explicit captain choice, only when even high effort is not enough.

rules.when: subtle root-cause work that calls for read-only diagnosis first: an intermittent bug, a concurrency or race condition, an algorithmic problem, a security or data-integrity issue, highly coupled reasoning across a system, or a problem that has already survived repeated attempts, where the immediate deliverable is finding the root cause rather than fixing it yet (the scout form). This is a difficulty-of-reasoning test, not a size test - many files touched does not imply DEEP, and a single concurrency bug can. If the work is mostly settled, broad execution rather than an unsettled reasoning problem, that is IMPLEMENT-LARGE instead; if the deliverable is a forward structural recommendation rather than a diagnosis, that is ARCHITECTURE instead; if the deliverable is adversarial challenge of someone else's plan or claim rather than your own diagnosis, that is TENTH-MAN instead. If Opus 5.5's own diagnosis pass needs an independent alternative or escalation, that is the Sol-escalation rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Opus 5.5 at xhigh is the active, single-candidate primary for the read-only diagnosis form: find the root cause, do not fix it yet. This is not a quota-resolved peer of the Sol-escalation rule below - Opus 5.5 is the default diagnosis route, Sol is reached for only when that rule's escalation condition genuinely applies.

rules.when: the same read-only DEEP diagnosis work above, specifically when the Opus 5.5 diagnosis rule above is not enough and an independent alternative or escalation, on a different model family and harness, is genuinely needed. This is a separate, more specific rule within DEEP, not a routine default: pick it only when that escalation condition genuinely applies, never as a first choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-sol on Pi is the independent alternative/escalation for DEEP diagnosis, deliberately kept on a different harness and model family from the OMP Opus 5.5 primary above, preserving the existing Pi placement for this escalation in the diagnosis form. openai-codex/gpt-6-astra remains available only through the separate, more specific exceptional rule below, once even this Sol escalation leaves the diagnosis unresolved.

rules.when: the same reasoning-difficulty DEEP work above, once the difficult implementation and its supporting tools are clean enough to diagnose and fix in one session (the ship form), rather than requiring a separate read-only diagnosis pass first. If the Opus 5.5 ship pass leaves the problem unresolved, that is the Sol second-hypothesis rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Opus 5.5 at xhigh is the active, single-candidate primary once diagnosis and the difficult implementation belong in the same mutating session. This is not a quota-resolved peer of the Sol second-hypothesis rule below - Opus 5.5 runs first, Sol is reached for only after that rule's condition genuinely applies.

rules.when: the same mutating DEEP ship work above, specifically as a second hypothesis once the Opus 5.5 ship pass above has run and the problem remains unresolved. This is a separate, more specific rule within DEEP, not a routine default: pick it only after the Opus 5.5 pass has genuinely failed to resolve the problem, never as a first choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-sol on OMP is reached for only as a second hypothesis once the Opus 5.5 ship pass above leaves the problem unresolved, preserving the existing OMP placement for this escalation in the ship form. openai-codex/gpt-6-astra remains available only through the separate, more specific exceptional rule below, once even this Sol second hypothesis leaves the problem unresolved.

rules.when: the same reasoning-difficulty DEEP work above, in either the scout or ship form, specifically as the last escalation once the relevant Sol escalation above (scout diagnosis or ship second hypothesis) has already run and the problem remains genuinely unresolved. This is a separate, more specific rule within DEEP, not a routine default and not a quota-resolved peer of any rule above: pick it only after a Sol escalation has genuinely failed to resolve the problem, never as a first or second choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-astra on Pi is DEEP's last escalation, reached for only once the Opus 5.5 primary and the Sol escalation above have both failed to resolve the problem. Astra stays limited to this and this configuration's other genuinely exceptional lanes across both the scout and ship forms; it is never a routine DEEP default.

rules.when: frontend or browser-visible behavior: forms, validation, navigation, interactive components, browser-side state, or end-to-end user flows where automated tests can pass while real user behavior is wrong. If there is no browser-visible behavior at stake, that is IMPLEMENT instead. If the underlying change is deep code-plus-browser work whose implementation is itself delicate, that is the Opus-escalation rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Sonnet at high effort, paired with this configuration's existing browser/manual verification policy (primary-policy.md section 7). Browser-visible surface alone is never a reason to reach for Opus or Astra as a default. If the underlying bug is a genuinely hard reasoning problem rather than an ordinary UI change, route it to DEEP instead and still apply browser verification to confirm the fix. Deep code-plus-browser work is a separate, more specific rule below, not a quota-resolved peer of this ordinary case.

rules.when: the same browser-visible UI/BROWSER work above, specifically when the underlying change is deep code-plus-browser work: delicate implementation (races, state machines, security-sensitive logic, or coordinated multi-file consistency) that must also be verified through the browser. This is a separate, more specific rule within UI/BROWSER, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick it only when the implementation itself is genuinely delicate, not merely because a UI is involved.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at high effort is reserved for UI/BROWSER work whose implementation is itself delicate enough to warrant it, still paired with this configuration's browser/manual verification policy (primary-policy.md section 7). Never a default for ordinary browser-visible changes.
